# Water:Fat in every patient {#sec-every-patient}


The same measurement for every patient from Nova 250 onwards. The analysis is done **per patient, comparing their two breasts**:

1. **Select the patients**: every Nova patient from Nova 250 onwards with at least one NORMAL, BENIGN or CANCER sample, after dropping those with a
   left/right image-total imbalance of 2× or more (@fig-intensity-imbalance).
2. **Mean each breast**: all of that breast's scans (every sample and set) are peak-shift corrected, min-max normalised and averaged into one curve.
   A breast whose scans carry more than one label is left out.
3. **Fit and measure**: two Gaussians are fitted to each breast's mean curve and its Water:Fat is worked out, as in @fig-water-fat.
   A breast whose scans stop before q ≈ 23 (so the water peak can't be fitted) is left out.
4. **Compare the two breasts**: for each patient with one breast of each kind (one CANCER and one NORMAL breast, say), we note whether the breast
   expected to have more water has the higher Water:Fat.
5. **Count and test**: the share of patients where it does, with a two-sided binomial test against 50%, which is what chance would give if
   Water:Fat said nothing about the tissue.

Each patient counts once, however many samples or scans they have.

::: {#cell-fig-all-patients .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# COMPARISONS, breast (Water:Fat of every breast) and pairs come from cohort_common
results = {}  # comparison: (patients whose first-named breast has the higher Water:Fat, patients compared, p-value)
for comparison, (base, others) in COMPARISONS.items():
    found = pairs(all_novas, base, others)
    higher = int(sum(other > base_ratio for base_ratio, other in found))
    results[comparison] = (higher, len(found), binomtest(higher, len(found)).pvalue)
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7  # small text so both panels fit side by side on an A4 page
fig, (pair_ax, share_ax) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
for ax in (pair_ax, share_ax):
    ax.set_box_aspect(1)  # square panels
for normal_ratio, cancer_ratio in pairs(all_novas, "NORMAL", ("CANCER",)):
    up = cancer_ratio > normal_ratio
    pair_ax.plot([0, 1], [normal_ratio, cancer_ratio], color=ne.STATUS_COLOURS["CANCER"] if up else "grey",
                 alpha=0.8 if up else 0.6, lw=1, marker="o", ms=3)
higher, total, p_value = results["CANCER vs NORMAL"]
pair_ax.set(xticks=[0, 1], xticklabels=["NORMAL breast", "CANCER breast"], xlim=(-0.3, 1.3), yscale="log", ylabel="Water:Fat",
            title=f"CANCER vs NORMAL: {higher} of {total} patients ({higher / total:.0%})\nhave the higher Water:Fat in the CANCER breast")
pair_ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")
pair_ax.set_yticks([0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10], ["0.2", "0.5", "1", "2", "5", "10"])
pair_ax.minorticks_off()

COLOURS = {"CANCER vs NORMAL": ne.STATUS_COLOURS["CANCER"], "BENIGN vs NORMAL": ne.STATUS_COLOURS["BENIGN"],
           "CANCER vs BENIGN": "tab:brown"}
for k, (comparison, (higher, total, p_value)) in enumerate(results.items()):
    share_ax.bar(k, 100 * higher / total, color=COLOURS[comparison], width=0.65)
    share_ax.text(k, 100 * higher / total + 2, f"{higher}/{total}\np = {p_value:.2g}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6)
share_ax.axhline(50, color="black", ls=":", lw=1)
share_ax.text(len(results) - 0.5, 51, "chance", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6)
share_ax.set(xticks=range(len(results)), ylim=(0, 100), ylabel="patients whose first-named breast\nhas the higher Water:Fat (%)",
             title="Every comparison")
share_ax.set_xticklabels([c.replace(" vs ", "\nvs ") for c in results], fontsize=6)
share_ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10
```

:::
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Key result: CANCER vs NORMAL"}
In **66%** of patients
(25 of 38) the CANCER breast has the higher Water:Fat.
:::

This is in the expected direction, but it is not a strong result. Chance alone would give 50%, so
66% is only modestly better, and in
13 of the 38 patients
(about 34%) it is the NORMAL breast that has the higher Water:Fat.
With this few patients the difference from chance is not statistically significant
(two-sided binomial test against 50%, p = 0\.073). Water:Fat hints that we are on the right track, but on its own
it is far from a reliable way to tell a CANCER breast from a NORMAL one.

The other comparisons are no stronger: BENIGN vs NORMAL 22/52 \(42%\)
(below chance) and CANCER vs BENIGN 15/24 \(62%\),
and none is statistically significant. These are across 251 patients from Nova 250 onwards after the intensity-imbalance filter.

## Why the result is weak: where the beam samples the breast

We think the main reason is *where* in the breast the scattering signal comes from. Most samples sit in the fatty part of @fig-cohort (right) and
@fig-by-cohort: the beam has passed mostly through adipose tissue. There are two reasons this should weaken the comparison.

1. **A fatty measurement is less likely to be near the tumour.** Most breast carcinomas arise in the terminal duct lobular units, which lie in the
   glandular tissue [[1]](#references) [[2]](#references), and tumours have been found to arise mainly in locally dense, fibroglandular areas of the breast [[3]](#references).
   Other studies, however, did not find that regional density predicts where a tumour will appear once overall density is accounted for [[4]](#references), so this is a tendency, not a rule.
2. **Fibrous/glandular tissue is where the tumour's structural changes are most prominent.** Tumours remodel the collagen of the surrounding fibrous stroma,
   making it denser and more aligned [[5]](#references), and X-ray scattering has picked up changes in collagen structure in and next to breast tumours
   [[6]](#references) [[7]](#references). A measurement through fat samples little of the tissue where these changes happen.

So targeting the fibrous/glandular part of the breast should make a measurement (1) more likely to be near the tumour and (2) more likely to be of tissue
that responds to it. @fig-by-cohort points the same way: the water-rich samples of each cohort grow wetter from NORMAL to BENIGN to CANCER. But
choosing patients by those samples after the fact is not a fair test (@sec-top-selection), so the idea needs a rule that treats both breasts the
same, which is what @sec-on-the-fly sets out.
